messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Farmer
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 76

He is a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working the land, rising before dawn with his wife to tend the farm, check the irrigation channels, and plan the day around the weather and the condition of the crops. He describes himself as steady and practical, a man who solves problems by doing the next necessary task. That way of living begins to change after his youngest child becomes gravely ill.

The illness starts with what he first thinks is a common fever. His child is tired, pale, and not eating, and at first he tells himself it will pass. But within days the child worsens, and he and his wife are thrown into the frightening rhythm of hospital visits, tests, waiting rooms, and long stretches where no one can tell them exactly what is happening. He remembers carrying his child in his arms at the clinic, feeling how light the small body has become, and noticing with horror that his child is too weak to protest. When the doctor finally explains that the child’s life is in danger, he says it is as if the air leaves the room. He can still hear the medical words, but they seem to come from far away. What he remembers most clearly is the sensation of standing still while everything essential in his life is suddenly at risk.

In the months that follow, he becomes obsessed with watching for signs of decline. He checks his child’s breathing at night, listens for coughs, and wakes repeatedly to make sure the child is still alive. He no longer sleeps in long stretches. Even when the immediate crisis passes, he cannot let his guard down. He carries a sense that disaster is waiting just beyond the edge of ordinary life, ready to return without warning. At the farm, he works mechanically, but his mind is rarely there. He walks the rows of plants and finds himself staring at the ground, realizing he has not absorbed anything he has seen. Tasks that used to feel familiar now require effort, and he makes mistakes he would normally catch at once. He forgets tools, loses track of conversations, and becomes irritated when his wife tries to ask simple questions.

He is especially troubled by reminders. A child coughing in the market makes his chest tighten. The smell of antiseptic from a clinic or medicine bottle can bring back the hospital corridor so vividly that he has to stop and steady himself. At night, he replays the worst moments in his mind: the doctor’s serious face, his child’s limp hand, the fear that he would lose the child before he had a chance to help. These images intrude without permission, often while he is trying to work or pray. He does not talk about them easily. In his family, he is used to being the one others depend on, and he feels ashamed by how helpless he felt when his child was sick. He worries that if he speaks about it too much, he will fall apart.

Since then, he has become more distant with others. He still fulfills his duties, but he no longer joins conversations the way he once did. He avoids stories about illness and becomes quiet when relatives ask about the child’s health. Even after the child improves, he cannot fully trust the recovery. He checks, reassures himself, then checks again. His wife notices that he startles more easily at sudden sounds, and that he grows tense when the phone rings unexpectedly. At times, he becomes angry over small things and then feels guilty for snapping. At other times, he seems flat and exhausted, as though all the feeling has been drained out of him.

What stands out most is how much effort he spends trying to keep the memory contained. He stays busy, works longer hours when he can, and avoids sitting alone because quiet gives the fear room to grow. Yet even in motion, he remains on alert, as if his body has not received the message that the emergency has passed. He lives with a persistent sense that the world can change in an instant, and that the safety of his family depends on his being watchful enough to stop it.
